transcript.text: Every time I put the oven on it runs for a few minutes and then the trip switch goes and half the house loses power. Reset it 3 times tonight. Hotpoint built-in, about 9 years old. What could cause this?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. An oven that runs for a few minutes and then trips your main switch (RCD) is almost probably caused by an internal electrical fault where electricity is 'leaking' to the metal casing. The most common cause in a 9-year-old Hotpoint is a heating element whose insulation has broken down, or possibly a loose/burnt mains connection at the back of the unit. Because this involves live mains voltage and a safety trip, you must stop using the oven immediately. Do not attempt to reset it again, as repeated tripping can damage your home's wiring or cause fire. You need to call a qualified gas-safe registered engineer (or a competent electrician if it is purely electric) to inspect and replace the faulty component.

reading.symptom: runs for a few minutes and then the trip switch goes and half the house loses power

plan: They asked: "What could cause this?" - answer that first.

Safety: a supply trip hazard is active. The fixed safety warning is shown separately, do not repeat it. It must not be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it: say that plainly. You may explain the likely cause and suggest checks that are safe with it switched off and unplugged, but never say or imply that a check could make it safe to use, or that they might not need an engineer.
Checks they have done and what they found: reset trip switch - did it 3 times tonight.
Already given by the customer, never ask for it again: make Hotpoint.
The fault they reported is: "runs for a few minutes and then the trip switch goes and half the house loses power". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.
They asked about something unsafe (repeated reset): do not explain how to do it; the fixed safety wording is shown separately. Offer the safe alternative.

Stage 2: the checks they reported did not fix it. Give the next check that best separates the remaining likely causes, or say what the likely faulty part is if the checks already point to one. Until a check has confirmed which part has failed, name it as the likely part and the check that would confirm it; do not tell them to buy, order or replace it.
